background.definition: The spleen is located in the left upper quadrant running from the 9th to the 12th ribs. It is an important component of the lymphatic system, helping to remove microorganisms from the blood, particularly protozoans and encapsulated bacteria such as Pneumococcus. Other functions of the spleen include removing old or damaged red blood cells and synthesizing antibodies.

list.listitem: The spleen is the most commonly injured organ in blunt abdominal trauma.

Blunt abdominal trauma is more common than penetrating trauma in the pediatric population, and motor vehicle accidents are the most common etiology. Splenic injury consists of approximately 45% of all visceral injuries.
The incidence of splenic injury peaks in teenage years and middle age.
The incidence of splenic injury ranges from 5.2% to 7.6% of blunt abdominal trauma.
Blunt trauma is the most common cause; less commonly, penetrating trauma is a cause of splenic rupture.
Rarely, iatrogenic trauma with colonoscopy or lithotripsy.

Certain medical conditions (ie, infectious mononucleosis and malaria) may increase the likelihood of rupture as splenomegaly increases the pressure on the splenic capsule. Patients with sickle cell disease (especially children, prior to autosplenectomy) in sequestration crises may also be at increased risk.

A meta-analysis of 845 patients with atraumatic splenic rupture identified 6 major etiological groups: neoplastic (30.3%), infectious (27.3%), inflammatory, noninfectious (20.0%), drug- and treatment-related (9.2%) and mechanical (6.8%) disorders. The most common treatment related etiology was colonoscopy.
Splenic injury also occurs in about 1% of patients undergoing colectomy.
Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography has also been reported to result in splenic rupture.
A systematic review of children with leukemia found that 61% had splenomegaly, putting them at risk for rupture.
Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is a rare cause of non-traumatic rupture of spleen.
Iinfrequent causes are reported in a review of case reports and include pancreatitis, Gaucher's disease and Wilson disease.
Delayed splenic rupture may occur following non-operative management in children with blunt abdominal trauma.
Multiple myeloma with extramedullary disease can cause capsular distension and increased vascular fragility,
Brucellosis and babesiosis can involve the spleen resulting in splenomegaly. This may increase the risk of spontaneous rupture.
COVID-19 infection has also been reported to cause atraumatic splenic rupture.
Splenic rupture is primarily due to penetrating or blunt abdominal trauma, though there are nontraumatic causes to consider as well.
Containing about 1 unit of blood, the spleen is the most vascular organ of the body and it's for this reason that splenic rupture possesses a potentially life-threatening situation.
Patients with infectious mononucleosis or acute malaria should avoid contact sports or other causes of abdominal trauma. C
Patient's undergoing splenectomy need to be vaccinated against encapsulated microorganisms such as pneumococcal pneumonia. B
Consider splenic rupture in any patient with persistent abdominal pain after blunt trauma. C
The bedside FAST examination is the best initial imaging study for diagnosis of suspected splenic injury. B
If FAST is negative, but suspicion is still high for splenic injury, order CT with IV contrast. B
If a CT scan with IV contrast shows an arterial blush, perform angiography in the stable patient for possible embolization depending on the grade of the rupture. B

As is the case for any medical or surgical patient, history and physical are the first step in guiding clinical decision making. In penetrating injuries, location of the injury will guide differential diagnoses. For any patient involved in a motor vehicle accident or other blunt traumatic event with abdominal pain, splenic injury should be considered.

In a patient with a history of infectious mononucleosis, sickle cell disease or malaria who complains of abdominal pain, splenic involvement must be considered, especially after trauma (even if low intensity).

Physical examination may reveal tenderness of the left upper quadrant, distension of the abdomen and a palpable spleen. In patients who are victims of a motor vehicle accident, ecchymoses across the mid-abdomen (also called seat-belt sign) may indicate small bowel or spleen involvement. If the lower ribs of the patients left side are broken the spleen may be involved as well.

Referred pain to the left shoulder from diaphragmatic nerve root involvement may also be present. Vital signs are important indicators to hemodynamic status. A patient with blunt trauma that is tachycardic and hypotensive should be evaluated urgently and imaged.

The Focused Abdominal Sonogram for Trauma (FAST) is generally the first radiologic test utilized in the emergency department because of its practicality and ease of use. See for more information about FAST.

The primary goal of FAST is to determine indirect evidence of an intra-abdominal injury, such as free fluid collection, or directly, solid organ injury. FAST is unable to determine if a bowel injury is present, unless there is gross hemorrhage.

The reported sensitivity of FAST for the detection of all reported organ injuries ranges from 0.44 to 0.95, with high specificity of 0.84 to 1.0. A comparison of FAST to CT reported only 55% sensitivity and 50% negative predictive value for intraabdominal injury in pediatric patients.

CT scan with IV contrast is the study of choice in the stable patient. A study found that the sensitivity of CT to detect splenic rupture was 86% with an accuracy of 96.1%. When a positive finding on CT scan, such as an arterial blush, has been made, staging can be determined and one can decide whether angiography is indicated.

Angiography is generally not recommended as the initial study to determine if splenic rupture is present. If a CT scan with IV contrast shows an arterial blush, order an angiogram. In the stable patient, this can be used for embolization depending on the grade of the rupture ().
Suspect splenic rupture in patients with persistent abdominal pain following blunt or penetrating abdominal trauma.

Evaluation should begin with stabilization of the patient and a bedside FAST exam. If abnormal, urgent surgical evaluation, and managment; if negative but suspicion for intraabdominal injury persists, consider CT with IV contrast.
Hemodynamic stability and grading () will help to determine whether treatment is medical (conservative) or surgical. A
The ATOMAC guidelines () should guide management of children with blunt liver or spleen trauma. A

A recent Cochrane review of a single small study concluded that there is no evidence to support the use of surgery over observation for people with abdominal trauma. It is therefore recommended that managment be guided by the patient's hemodynamic status, and not the imaging findings alone.
Hemodynamically unstable patients with Grade 3 or greater lesions should undergo operative management via splenectomy.

A study found that 1.4% of children not undergoing splenectomy for rupture were readmitted in a 180-day period for surgical treatment. On average, the delayed bleeding was found 10 days after the initial event.

A systematic review identified reports of 186 cases of splenic rupture and 29 of splenic infarction. Six of 29 with infarction had an underlying hematologic condition such as sickle cell disease. Patients with a higher World Society of Emergency Surgery splenic rupture score were more likely to have operative management than those with a moderate or mild score (84% vs 58%, p = 0.001. The overall mortality of rupture was 4.8%.
Hemodynamically stable patients with Grade 1 and Grade 2 lesions may be treated conservatively, generally with serial CBC for hemoglobin and hematocrit counts.
In children, a study found that recombinant factor VIIa may be beneficial.
Arterial embolization is an option for hemodynamically stable patients with Grade 3 or greater lesions.
Failure of non operative management in patients with blunt splenic injury is more common over the age of 40 and in patients with more severe injury by validated scales of injury.
Delayed bleeding, though rare, may occur on average 10 days after conservative management. B
Grade 1 and Grade 2 splenic injury prognosis remains excellent. Prognosis worsens as the injury grade increases. C
Asplenic patients are at increased risk of fatal and debilitating infection for the remainder of their lives, and should therefore receive immunization. C
Nonoperative management is less effective in patients older than 55 years. The mortality is increased in these patients as well. C

feature.caption: Grading of Splenic Ruptures.
feature.feature_body:
Grade 1 Minor subcapsular tear or hematoma
Grade 2 Parenchymal injury not extending to the hilum
Grade 3 Major parenchymal injury involving vessels and hilum
Grade 4 Shattered spleen
*Adapted from Yang et al. (2008).

feature.caption: FAST Examinations.
feature.feature_body: A FAST examination consists of 4 different projections (): Longitudinal view of the right upper quadrant to visualize Morrison's pouch Transverse view of the subxiphoid region to visualize the inferior aspect of the pericardium to diagnose pericardial effusion or hemopericardium Longitudinal view of the left upper quadrant to visualize the splenorenal recess Transverse view of the suprapubic region to visualize either the rectouterine or rectovesical pouch An eFAST (extended FAST) is obtained after by adding anterior thoracic views of both lungs to look for pneumothorax.
